summary:
I've been building Claude-Orbiter, a desktop app for running several Claude agents at once on a visual canvas — cards for terminals, editors, browsers, and orchestrated multi-agent workflows. Most of the real work has been debugging the orchestration layer itself: agent cards that shared a parent process needed every stop/retry/kill action routed through the parent, not the sub-agent, or the whole thing silently deadlocked. One bug took a while to track down — two failing phases both called the same shared "brain" card at once, and because its callback queue only kept one slot, the second caller's result just vanished. Fixed it with a proper request queue so concurrent calls serialize instead of clobbering each other.

Underneath a few of my other projects is Switchboard, a small proxy that serializes access to a single GPU across a half-dozen consumers — an LLM brain, a chat backend, an image generator — since only one big model fits in memory at a time. The interesting problem was making swaps between models cheap: instead of a cold reload every time something else needed the card, I added save/restore of the model's KV cache state around each eviction, so a model coming back gets its short-term memory back instead of re-processing 20K tokens of context from scratch.

I've also been building a Japanese-learning app for myself from scratch — spaced-repetition drills, then reading passages, then a listening/dialogue layer once the basics held up. The one finding worth mentioning: I went looking for a way to give pronunciation feedback and ran three different transcription models against real recordings. All three correctly told sibilant sounds apart, but all three failed on a specific vowel-shift confusion, even at the largest model size — turns out that particular failure was an artifact of the synthetic training audio, not something a bigger model fixes. It reframed the feature: general pronunciation grading isn't reliable off the shelf, so what shipped was narrower and honest about it — timing and specific contrasts, not a blanket accuracy score.

On BudgetTracker, the design choice I'd point to is the ledger: money-related figures are append-only, so a correction never rewrites history, it just adds an offsetting entry next to the original. It sounds like a small thing, but it means the balance is always just "sum every entry," with nothing to get subtly wrong later.

highlights.oneLiner: Desktop app for running multiple Claude agents on a canvas; fixed a shared-callback race that dropped concurrent results
GPU proxy serializing one card across several consumers; added KV-cache save/restore to make model swaps cheap
Append-only ledger design: corrections add offsetting entries instead of rewriting history
